p: Codex Alexandrinus leaves out "were not filled"; Swete prints it from Codex Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, from Codex Venetus (V)
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it

why: Without the verb the question has no main verb at all, so A has lost words by a copying slip. Swete supplies them from V, and the Plain follows his text.

a: The old man was led away, his head thick with gray hair.
t: One old man, or a crowd of old men?
p: Codex Alexandrinus has "an old man full of gray hair"; Codex Venetus "a crowd of old men, gray-haired."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: an old man full of gray hair, thickly covered
readings.plain: The old man was led away, his head thick with gray hair.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: a crowd of old men, gray
readings.plain: A crowd of gray-haired old men was led away.

why: The Plain follows Swete's text, which takes the old man as one figure standing for many. V's plural makes the same point openly; Brenton's English ("a multitude of aged hoary-haired men") follows that reading. Both codices then have a plural participle (pepykasmenōn), so the verse was disturbed early.

a: This was not for the forced labor mentioned a little earlier.
t: Not for labor, or for labor?
p: Codex Venetus turns the denial into a statement: the register was for forced labor.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: οὐκ εἰς τὴν ἔμπροσθεν βραχεῖ προδεδηλωμένην τῶν ἔργων κατὰ τρόπον λατρείαν
readings.en: not for the service of labor shown a little before
readings.plain: This was not for the forced labor mentioned a little earlier.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: for (it was) for the toilsome service
readings.plain: It was for the hard labor mentioned a little earlier, and

why: A's reading fits the next clause, "but so that they could be tortured," which needs a "not" before it. V's "for" and "toilsome" look like a scribe smoothing a hard sentence.

a: , and he said things against God that were not fit to be said.
p: Swete adds "God" in brackets; Codex Alexandrinus has no object, and Codex Venetus lacks the whole clause.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with τὸν θεόν supplied in square brackets
readings.orig: εἰς δὲ [τὸν θεὸν] τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα λαλῶν
readings.en: and speaking against [God] what was not fitting
readings.plain: , and he said things against God that were not fit to be said.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it
readings.orig: εις δε τα μη καθ. λαλων
readings.en: and speaking for things not fitting
readings.plain: , and he said things that were not fit to be said.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. His bracket shows that he supplied "God" for the sense; A's "against things not fitting" is hard Greek. Brenton's English reads "against the Greatest God."

p: Codex Venetus adds a word: the king is testing his Kinsmen as if they were senseless.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: how long will you test us so

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.plain: keep testing us as if we had no sense

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. V's extra word (spelled oddly, allogous, for alogous, "senseless") is behind Brenton's "as of men bereft of reason."

a: well known among the Jews of the countryside
p: Codex Venetus makes Eleazar "well known among the priests of the country."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: ἐπίσημος τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χώρας Ἰουδαίων
readings.en: notable among the Jews from the country
readings.plain: well known among the Jews of the countryside

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; Brenton's English ("an illustrious priest of the country")
readings.plain: well known among the priests of the countryside

why: The Plain follows Swete's text. V's "priests" may come from the priestly name Eleazar, or from the memory of other priestly Eleazars; Brenton's English follows it.

p: In Codex Alexandrinus a later hand wrote "under Pharaoh" over an erasure where Swete prints "Father, you, Pharaoh."

readings.w: Swete's printed text
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), corrected by a later hand over an erasure, as Swete's notes report it

why: The corrector's "under Pharaoh" does not fit the sentence, whose verb is "you destroyed" with Pharaoh as its object. Swete's "Father, you" matches the form of the other rescues, which each begin "you" (6:5, 6, 7), and the prayer's address to God as Father (6:8).

a: You made the red-hot furnace wet with dew, and you rescued them,
p: Codex Venetus has no dew: "you rescued them from the furnace burning so long."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.en: having bedewed the fiery furnace, you rescued
readings.plain: You made the red-hot furnace wet with dew, and you rescued them,

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: from the long-burning fiery furnace you rescued
readings.plain: You rescued them from the furnace that had burned red-hot so long,

why: A's "dew" agrees with the Greek Daniel (Greek Daniel 3:50), which this prayer follows, and Brenton's English has "a dewy coolness." V's "long-burning" may be a scribe's change of an unfamiliar verb. The Plain follows A and Swete.

p: Codex Venetus calls God "Protector of all" instead of "Judge of all."

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: Both words fit the prayer: God judges the arrogant and protects the weak. The Plain follows Swete's text.

p: Codex Alexandrinus has "time" (chronon), Swete prints "dance" (choron) with a corrector of Venetus.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with the corrector of Codex Venetus (Va)
readings.en: having formed the dance already mentioned

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it

why: The words differ by one letter. "The dance we spoke of" points back to 6:32, where the Jews "formed dances"; A's "the time we spoke of" has no clear reference, so it is a copying slip.

p: Codex Venetus has "our affairs" (pragmata) for "our decrees" (prostagmata).

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: κατευθύνοντος ἡμῖν τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ τὰ προστάγματα
readings.en: the great God directing our decrees

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: V's "affairs" is the usual phrase of royal letters (compare 3:13, "so are our affairs"). A's "decrees" is the harder reading and fits the irony: the God who now guides the king's decrees is undoing the first one. The Plain follows Swete.

p: Codex Venetus says they "punished" the renegades, not that they "killed" them.

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it

why: Both codices agree in the next clause that "they put them to death" (anēiroun), and both say three hundred were killed (7:15), so V's softer verb does not change the event. The Plain follows Swete.

p: Swete's text reads "holy Savior." Alexandrinus has "of the holy ones, to you," and Venetus "eternal."

readings.w: Swete's printed text
Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as Swete's notes report it
readings.en: of the holy ones, to you

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; Brenton's English ("the eternal Saviour of Israel")

why: A's letters (hagiōn soi) look like a miscopying of hagiōi sōtēri, which Swete prints; V has "eternal" instead. Swete's text is not here the reading of either codex as it stands. The Plain follows it.

p: Codex Alexandrinus breaks off at "each to the"; the Plain follows Codex Venetus, "each to his own."

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; Brenton's English
readings.orig: εκαστος εις την + ιδιαν· και πλειστην
readings.en: each to his own (land); and very great (authority than before)

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))

why: A's sentence has lost words: "each to the" runs straight into "before, among the enemies" (7:21). V supplies "his own" and, for 7:21, "very great" authority, "more" than before. The Plain follows V here and says so, and the next verse depends on the same reading (see 7:21).

a: They had more authority than before among their enemies
p: This reading goes with 7:20. Codex Venetus has "very great" authority; Alexandrinus only "before."

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it (καὶ πλείστην, at the end of 7:20)
readings.plain: They had more authority than before among their enemies

readings.w: Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))
readings.orig: ἔμπροσθεν, ἐν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς ἐξουσίαν ἐσχηκότες
readings.en: before, having authority among the enemies
readings.plain: They had authority among their enemies

why: Without V's words A's text does not make a full sentence. Brenton's English ("they had more weight than before among their enemies") follows the same reading as the Plain.

p: Codex Venetus reads "fear" (phobou); Alexandrinus and Swete "payment" (phorou), one letter apart.

readings.w: Codex Venetus (V), as Swete's notes report it; Brenton's English ("with the greatest terror")
Swete's printed text (Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD))

why: The Plain departs from Swete here. "Fear" matches 7:21 ("with glory and awe") and the common pattern of enemies who fear the rescued (Esther 8:17); "tribute" is hard to fit, since the goods are only being returned. The two words differ by one letter.
